strengths: Addresses a relevant and clearly motivated problem: combining 2D/3D multimodal reasoning with physically feasible planning for embodied agents, framed via two well-articulated gaps (geometric adaptability, embodiment constraint).

The Task-Adaptive Gated Router is a sensible mechanism for conditional 3D feature injection, and the paper provides both quantitative ablations (Table 1) and interpretable qualitative analysis of gate activation (Figures 4-5), which strengthens the credibility of the design.

The two-stage training paradigm (SFT warm-up followed by TE-GRPO with task and embodiment rewards and a progressive curriculum) is well-motivated, and the ablation in Figure 6 isolates the contribution of r_task and r_embod on both primitive skills and downstream simulated manipulation tasks.

Unusually broad evaluation: 8 public benchmarks spanning image/video/3D modalities, object navigation on HM3D/MP3D, simulator-based end-to-end mobile manipulation, and real-world robot deployment examples — beyond what most comparable MLLM papers provide.

Strong reported results: SOTA on 7/8 public benchmarks with an 8B model against much larger baselines (RoboBrain-2.0-32B, GPT-4o, Gemini-2.5-Pro), plus competitive 3D grounding without external detection modules.
Substantial implementation and dataset detail in the appendix (5.2M training samples, hyperparameters, benchmark construction), supporting reproducibility.
weaknesses: Novelty is moderate: conditional/dynamic 3D feature fusion is closely related to mixture-of-experts and existing adaptive-injection ideas, and the embodiment-aware component is essentially reward shaping on top of GRPO (Shao et al., 2024). The claim of being the 'first framework' to dynamically integrate 2D and 3D inputs is overstated without more careful differentiation from prior adaptive-routing work.

The headline ablation gain of the TAGR module is small (+1.22% average over hard-coded 3D integration, Table 1), which undercuts the emphasis placed on this contribution; no variance, seeds, or statistical significance are reported anywhere, and several per-benchmark differences (e.g., 62.35 vs 62.15 on SQA3D) appear within noise.

A significant portion of the strongest evidence comes from four self-designed benchmarks (Where2Go/Where2Fit/Where2Approach/Where2Grasp) and self-built simulation tasks, evaluated against baselines not specifically trained for them; there is a risk the evaluation design favors the proposed model, and no independent or third-party embodiment benchmark is used for the feasibility claims.

The TE-GRPO evaluation relies on an EvalExec reward computed within a simulator, but the paper acknowledges the embodiment reward yields no significant gain for Mobile Pickup and provides limited detail on how r_embod is actually computed (kinematic/reachability checks) in the main text, making it hard to assess generality.

Writing and consistency issues: the module is referred to as both 'TAGR' and 'TGGR' (Figure 5 discussion), a stray 'huozh' appears in Appendix A.2.2, Figure 1's '7 out of 8' framing papers over the ScanRefer result, and some benchmark numbers in the text vs. tables are not always trivially reconcilable.

The end-to-end pipeline's dependence on the low-level control policy bottleneck (grasping) is acknowledged but not resolved; real-robot results are only qualitative photo sequences with no success-rate statistics, so the 'physically executable plans' claim rests mostly on simulator evidence.

No comparison against strong recent reasoning/reinforcement-tuned baselines (e.g., other GRPO-style post-trained VLMs) to isolate whether gains come from the embodiment-aware rewards or simply from additional RL post-training.

strengths: Broad empirical coverage: evaluation spans 8 public benchmarks (2D, video, and 3D), object navigation on HM3D/MP3D, simulator-based mobile manipulation tasks, and real robot deployment, which is unusually comprehensive for an 8B embodied model.

The Task-Adaptive Gated Router (TAGR) is a sensible idea for avoiding hard-coded 3D injection, and the paper includes an ablation against both hard-coded and no-3D baselines (Table 1) as well as interpretability analyses of gate activation (Figures 4-5).

The TE-GRPO reward design with a progressive embodiment curriculum (Equations 8-10) is a reasonable mechanism for shifting optimization from semantic correctness to physical feasibility, and the ablation in Figure 6 shows consistent gains from the reward components on both primitive benchmarks and downstream execution tasks.
Extensive appendix documentation of training data (~5.2M samples), hyperparameters, and benchmark construction supports transparency about the training pipeline.
weaknesses: The headline contribution is modest: the core novelty is conditional 3D feature injection via a gated router plus reward shaping on GRPO. The reported benefit of the router itself is small (Table 1: +1.22% average over hard-coded 3D integration, better on only 3 of 4 tasks, and on ScanQA it is worse than hard-coded integration), so the 'first framework to dynamically integrate 2D and 3D' claim is oversold relative to the evidence.

The strong SOTA claims are confounded by scale and data mixture: OmniEVA is trained on a large, curated 5.2M-sample mixture including many of the evaluation domains, while the closest competitor (RoboBrain-2.0-32B) is not trained on the same data. No controlled comparison isolates how much of the +10.45 average gain comes from the architectural contributions versus the data recipe.

In-house benchmarks (Where2Go/Fit/Approach/Grasp) are constructed by the authors from HM3D/MP3D data that also underpins the 3D training data (3D Subgoal Prediction uses HM3D/MP3D in Habitat), raising potential train/test overlap concerns that are not explicitly ruled out.

The gate analysis is not convincing: the case study probabilities (0.73, 0.52, 0.39, 0.38) barely deviate from the Bernoulli(0.5) prior the model is regularized toward, so 'activated' at 0.52 is essentially noise; also TAGR is frozen after pretraining, so the gate never adapts during SFT/GRPO, which is a questionable and under-justified design choice. Inference uses Gumbel temperature 1e-6, making the 'soft' formulation essentially deterministic.

Real-world experiments are purely qualitative (Appendix F figures) with no success rates or sample sizes, despite executability being a central claim; the paper itself concedes r_embod gives no significant gain for Mobile Pickup.

Writing and polish issues throughout undermine confidence: typos ('OminiEVA', 'denodes', 'TGGR module' vs 'TAGR', 'Dectivated', 'rendcent', 'Moile Placement'), a missing project page URL after the abstract claims one, stray text in the appendix ('...complex 3D environments.huozh'), and Equation 5's 'MoE interpretation' is algebraically trivial and misleading. The 'Huawei Proprietary - Restricted Distribution' watermark is in tension with reproducibility.
No error bars, significance tests, or multiple seeds for any benchmark; several SOTA margins are small (e.g., +0.3 on ScanQA) and could fall within noise.

The Gumbel-Softmax formulation and frozen-gate design leave an unclear picture of how the router is trained and used in practice, and there is no analysis of gate behavior on the embodiment tasks where it matters most.

strengths: The paper addresses two clearly motivated gaps in MLLM-based embodied reasoning (rigid 3D injection vs. no 3D, and plans ignoring physical/embodiment constraints), and the two proposed mechanisms (TAGR gated router and TE-GRPO) map directly onto these gaps.

Evaluation breadth is impressive: 8 public benchmarks spanning 2D image-, video-, and 3D-based reasoning, plus four newly proposed primitive embodied benchmarks, end-to-end simulator evaluation (object navigation on HM3D/MP3D, mobile manipulation), and real-robot deployment examples.

The controlled comparison in Table 1 (hard-coded 3D vs. no 3D vs. dynamic gating, trained on identical data) isolates the contribution of the gating mechanism, and the qualitative/quantitative analysis of gate activation behavior (Figures 4-5) provides interpretability.

TE-GRPO is a sensible extension of GRPO with a curriculum-style reward scheduling from semantic correctness to physical feasibility, and the ablation (Figure 6) shows both reward terms contribute individually and synergistically, with an honest discussion of where gains saturate due to low-level control bottlenecks.

The training data curation (5.2M samples across general, image, video, and 3D reasoning) is documented in detail in the appendix, and implementation details (hyperparameters, voxelization, frame sampling) support reproducibility of the training pipeline.
weaknesses: The headline benefit of the core novelty (TAGR) is small: the dynamic 3D integration improves over hard-coded integration by only ~1.22% on average (Table 1), and on some benchmarks it is essentially on par with or worse than simpler baselines (e.g., ScanQA, Scan2Cap are close; ScanRefer slightly trails). The significance of this gain is not statistically validated.

Three of the four primitive benchmarks (Where2Go, Where2Fit, Where2Approach, Where2Grasp) are small (200-464 samples) and self-proposed by the authors, and the evaluation sets are constructed from the same simulators/scene sources (HM3D, MP3D) used to build the custom training data, raising concerns about train/test domain overlap and self-favorable evaluation.

The video spatial reasoning training data is explicitly built 'aligned with the task taxonomy defined by VSI-Bench' from ScanNet/Matterport3D — the same sources underlying VSI-Bench — creating potential contamination that is not adequately discussed or controlled for.

Real-world experiments are purely qualitative (two example prompts, photo sequences); no quantitative success rates, number of trials, or failure analysis are reported, which weakens the central claim of improved 'executability' on physical robots.

Key details of the TE-GRPO rewards are underspecified: how EvalTask and EvalExec are implemented (rule-based vs. LLM judge), how kinematic/reachability constraints are validated in the simulator, and how the model's point outputs interface with the low-level control policy.

TAGR is frozen after pretraining, but there is no ablation on the router's conditioning signals (task-only vs. scene-only vs. both), nor on the Gumbel-Softmax temperature schedule or the KL prior, so the design choices are not justified empirically.

Novelty claims ('pioneers', 'first framework') are somewhat overstated; conditional/dynamic injection of auxiliary modalities and reward-shaped RL fine-tuning are established ideas, and the paper does not position against closely related adaptive-fusion or RLHF-style embodied planning work.

The project page is empty ('Project page:' with no URL), no code or model release is confirmed, and there are editorial sloppiness issues (inconsistent naming 'TAGR' vs. 'TGGR', 'Omini-Supervised' typo, stray text 'huozh' in Appendix A.2.2), which hurts polish and reproducibility.
